106	## 3. Ground Truths
107	
108	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
109	
110	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
111	
112	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
113	
114	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
115	
116	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
117	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
118	
119	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
120	
121	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
122	
123	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
124	
125	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
126	
127	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
128	
129	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
130	
131	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a HIGH-confidence chain, name its read-at-source location. Write the list, not a number:
132	
133	```text
134	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
135	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
136	```
137	
138	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
139	
140	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.

144	## 4. Derivation Chains
145	
146	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
147	
148	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
149	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
150	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
151	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
152	
153	**Chain format:**
154	
155	```text
156	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
157	```
158	
159	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
160	
161	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
162	
163	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
164	
165	```text
166	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
167	→ [intermediate claim]
168	→ [further intermediate]
169	→ [conclusion]
170	```
171	
172	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
173	
174	```text
175	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
176	→ [intermediate claim]
177	→ [conclusion]
178	```
179	
180	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
181	
182	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
183	
184	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
185	
186	```text
187	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
188	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
189	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
190	```
191	
192	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
193	
194	```text
195	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
196	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
197	  once idle-time billing is included
198	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
199	```
200	
201	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
202	
203	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
204	
205	```text
206	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
207	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
208	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
209	```
210	
211	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
212	
213	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
214	
215	```text
216	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
217	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
218	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
219	```
220	
221	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
222	
223	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
224	
225	```text
226	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
227	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
228	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
229	```
230	
231	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
232	
233	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
234	
235	```text
236	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
237	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
238	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
239	```
240	
241	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
242	
243	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
244	
245	```text
246	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
247	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
248	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
249	```
250	
251	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
252	
253	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
254	
255	```text
256	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
257	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
258	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
259	```
260	
261	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
262	
263	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
264	
265	```text
266	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
267	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
268	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
269	```
270	
271	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
272	
273	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
274	
275	```text
276	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
277	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
278	→ the second reading is the binding one
279	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
280	```
281	
282	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
283	
284	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
285	
286	```text
287	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
288	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
289	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
290	```
291	
292	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
293	
294	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
295	
296	```text
297	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
298	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
299	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
300	```
301	
302	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
303	
304	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
305	
306	```text
307	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
308	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
309	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
310	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
311	```
312	
313	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
314	
315	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
316	
317	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
318	
319	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
320	
321	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
322	
323	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
324	
325	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
326	
327	```text
328	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
329	```
330	
331	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
332	
333	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
334	
335	```text
336	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
337	```
338	
339	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
340	
341	### Confidence levels, defined
342	
343	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
344	
345	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
346	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
347	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
348	
349	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
350	
351	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
352	
353	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
354	
355	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
356	
357	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
358	
359	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
360	
361	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
362	
363	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
364	
365	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
366	
367	```text
368	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
369	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
370	```
371	
372	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
373	
374	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
375	
376	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
377	
378	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
379	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
380	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
381	
382	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
383	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
384	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
385	
386	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. For each downgrade cause belonging to the chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — the line states what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists. A stated reason is the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause; "speculative" is never such a reason. The validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause is the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, and naming any other clause, including the speculative EXCEPT clause, stands in for nothing. A chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing, so the rubric's speculative EXCEPT clause no longer covers it, and the cited chain's own confidence line states its verification path; a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another chain's head, and stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (§5).

390	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
391	
392	Record every reasoning path that was explored and discarded. This section is required in every analysis. Dead ends are not failures — they are part of the reasoning record and save future analysts from re-exploring paths that have already been ruled out.
393	
394	### Dead End: [Name of discarded path]
395

381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.

387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. 570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.

575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.

581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.

594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.

A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about Roediger and Karpicke's research on the testing effect, retrieval practice, and long-term retention:

## Key Findings

The phenomenon termed the 'testing effect' or 'retrieval-based learning' refers to the substantial gains in long-term retention of material resulting from active retrieval of information during learning. Tests enhance later retention more than additional study of the material, even when tests are given without feedback.

## Notable Studies

Roediger and Karpicke (2006a) investigated the effects of single versus multiple testing events on long-term retention using educationally relevant conditions, with the goal of determining whether any connection existed between the number of times students were tested and the size of the testing effect.

In one experiment, repeated testing during learning enhanced retention relative to repeated studying, although alternating study and test trials produced the best retention.

## Long-Term Retention Benefits

Repeatedly studying material is beneficial for tests given soon after learning, but on delayed criterial tests with retention intervals measured in days or weeks, prior testing can produce greater performance than prior studying, with test trials producing a much greater gain than study trials.

Karpicke and Roediger (2008) showed that students who engaged in repeated retrieval practice retained significantly more information on delayed tests than students who spent the same time re-reading material.

Here are the key findings from research studies on Turnitin's AI detection accuracy and false positive rates:

## Turnitin's Claims vs. Independent Studies

Turnitin has publicly stated that its AI writing detection achieves roughly 98% accuracy with a false-positive rate under 1%, for documents where more than 20% of the text is AI-generated. However, this figure describes Turnitin's own internal testing methodology and conditions; it is not an independent, peer-reviewed measurement.

## Major Independent Studies (2023-2024)

**Stanford Research (2023):**
The most widely cited independent evaluation is Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, and Zou (Stanford University), published in the journal Patterns in 2023. The study ran seven GPT detectors against 91 TOEFL essays written by non-native English speakers and found an average false-positive rate of 61.3% across those detectors.

**Recent Peer-Reviewed Studies (2024):**
A 2024 study published in the journal "Computers and Education" tested Turnitin against a dataset of 500 human-written and 500 AI-generated essays. The researchers found Turnitin correctly flagged AI text 91% of the time, but the false positive rate for human text was 4.2%.

## Concerning Disparities

False-positive rates on non-native English writing, heavily-edited drafts, and technical prose climb to 5–12% in peer-reviewed and university-conducted studies. Recent studies also indicate that neurodivergent students (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, etc…) and students for whom English is a second language are flagged by AI detection tools at higher rates than native English speakers.

The research clearly shows significant discrepancies between Turnitin's claimed accuracy and real-world independent testing results.

## Definition and Overview

Contract cheating is the commissioning of bespoke university assignments with the intention of submitting them for assessment. ## Industry Scale

The prevalence of essay mills and other types of sites offering help to students is concerning, with highly organised business structures. Academic dishonesty is increasing, with essay mills a prominent contributory factor.

# AI Text Detector False-Positive Rates

## Key Findings on Non-Native English Speakers

The most significant independent research comes from Stanford University. Researchers Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, and Zou published findings in *Patterns* (2023) examining seven GPT detectors tested against 91 TOEFL essays from non-native English speakers. ## Why Non-Native Writers Are Disproportionately Flagged

The page explains that second-language academic writing exhibits characteristics detectors interpret as AI-generated: "second-language academic writing often relies on a narrower, more standard vocabulary and more templated sentence construction." These statistical markers—low sentence-length variation and high word predictability—trigger false flags.

## Vendor Claims vs. Independent Results

Turnitin claims approximately 98% accuracy with under 1% false positives, but only "for documents where more than 20% of the text is AI-generated." This represents internal testing under controlled conditions and doesn't reflect real-world performance on diverse student populations.

The contrast illustrates why institutions increasingly require corroborating evidence beyond detector scores alone.

# Key Finding on Repeated Retrieval Practice

Based on this research paper, repeated retrieval practice (testing) produces substantially better long-term retention compared to repeated studying.

The critical quantitative finding shows that **students who took repeated tests retained approximately 80% of material after one week, while those who only restudied retained around 36%** of the same information. This dramatic difference—more than doubling retention—demonstrates that the testing effect substantially enhances memory persistence over time.

The paper's core conclusion is that retrieval practice during the learning phase creates more durable memories than passive review, even when the total study time remains constant. This finding has significant implications for educational practice, suggesting that assessment strategies based on retrieval (like quizzing and testing) should be prioritized over additional studying for maximizing long-term retention.

# The Analysis

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** What decision rule should govern whether a specific university course replaces its timed written exam with a take-home assessment, given that LLM writing assistants can now perform much of the unaided-writing task those exams were built to certify?

The question as commonly posed — "should the university switch?" — treats the policy choice as a single, global, binary decision. Stripped of that framing, the real question is narrower and more useful: for a given course, which format (and under what conditions) validly certifies the specific competency that course exists to certify. "Timed exam vs. take-home" turns out to be a proxy for at least two underlying design axes — how much time-pressure the task imposes, and how much tool/AI access it permits — and the right setting on those axes depends on what is being certified, not on a university-wide policy preference.

**Success criteria:**
1. The Conclusion names, for at least two distinct competency types, which assessment format each type should use, and the criterion that distinguishes them.
2. The Conclusion states what happens to the claim "timed exams guarantee integrity while take-home cannot," and grounds that statement in a derivation chain rather than an assertion.
3. The Conclusion names at least one institutional precondition — beyond the format choice itself — required for the recommended policy to remain valid over time.
4. A reader can apply the Conclusion's decision rule to a course not explicitly discussed in this analysis (e.g., "a sophomore organic chemistry course," "a graduate creative-writing workshop") without needing to ask the author for further clarification.

---

## 2. Assumptions Table

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1. Timed written exams accurately measure real-world competence | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — true only for the subset of competencies where unaided, time-pressured performance is itself the certified skill (see C3); false as a general claim | unverified — flagged (used, scoped, in C3) |
| A2. Take-home = AI-assisted cheating is undetectable | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Challenge — overstated; GT-2 shows automated *detection* is unreliable, not that authorship is unverifiable by any means (oral defense and process logs corroborate) | unverified — flagged (used, qualified, in C1/C2) |
| A3. AI writing assistants are purely a threat to assessment integrity, not also a tool students will use post-graduation | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — contradicted by GT-11? and by the post-graduation-relevance criterion in C2/C3 | unverified — flagged (GT-11?) |
| A4. Only timed, proctored exams can guarantee individual attribution of work | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Discard — ruled out by C1: no format achieves certainty, only bounded confidence | verified via GT-9 (definitional) and GT-2 (read-at-source) |
| A5. Switching fully to take-home solves the equity concerns raised by timed exams | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Challenge — partially true (removes the test-anxiety penalty, GT-8?) but introduces new inequities (device/AI-subscription access, home environment); net effect is redistribution, not elimination (Adversarial pass, Cluster 4) | unverified — flagged |
| A6. A university's assessment purpose is uniform across all courses and disciplines | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — contradicted by GT-7?, which the C2/C3 divergence itself demonstrates | unverified — flagged (GT-7?) |
| A7. If AI can produce competent output for a task, the human skill behind it is no longer worth certifying | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Discard — conflates the old skill (unaided production) with a new one (directing/evaluating AI output), which C2's redesigned take-home certifies rather than abandons | unverified — flagged |
| A8. The policy choice is binary: timed exam or take-home | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Discard — the real design space is at least two-dimensional (time-boxing × tool/AI access); C2's "redesigned take-home" and C3's "open-book timed exam" both sit off the pure binary | verified by construction (four scored options, not two) |
| A9. AI-detection software is a viable long-term primary integrity control for take-home assessments | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Discard as primary control — GT-2's 61.3% average false-positive rate on non-native-speaker writing (vs. near-zero on native writing) makes it an unreliable and discriminatory primary signal; retained only as a weak secondary signal (Dead End 3, §5) | verified via GT-2 (read-at-source) |
| A10. Faculty grading capacity and integrity infrastructure can absorb a full switch to take-home without added cost | current constraint | Accept — expires the moment take-home adoption exceeds current faculty/TA capacity for spot-checks or oral defense; true only where an institution invests in that capacity | Accept — expires at the point verification demand exceeds current staffing, unless new capacity is funded | unverified — flagged (used in C4) |
| A11. GT-1's testing-effect advantage, established mainly for cued recall of word lists and short passages, transfers to full essay- and argument-length timed writing | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Challenge — plausible but not confirmed by the cited studies, which tested a narrower recall task than a full essay exam; retained as an explicit, priced premise in C3 | unverified — flagged (used in C3) |
| A12. A course's own stated learning outcomes, not some external standard, are the correct reference point for judging construct validity | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Accept — the alternative (an externally imposed, generic standard) is less defensible course-by-course and matches standard outcome-based accreditation practice | unverified — flagged (used in C2) |
| A13. The assigned criterion weights (construct validity 5, integrity 4, equity 4, feasibility 3, post-graduation relevance 3) reflect this institution's actual priorities | convention | Explicitly challenge before use | Challenge — a genuine value choice specific to this illustrative analysis; a real institution must re-weight for its own context, though the flip-test results in C2/C3 show the ranking is fairly robust to reasonable variation | unverified — flagged (used in C2/C3) |
| A14. Administrators facing implementation confusion are more likely to simplify toward a uniform policy than to invest further in a differentiated one | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Challenge — a behavioral prediction about institutional response, not independently evidenced here; it is the premise the Adversarial pass's Cluster 1/3 disposition is designed to prevent from becoming true | unverified — flagged (used in C4) |
| A15. Employers and prospective students can perceive and value a credible "fundamentals-strong and AI-fluent" signal over a generic degree | untested belief | Verify or flag as unverified | Challenge — plausible given GT-11? but not independently confirmed | unverified — flagged (used in C4) |
| A16. Syllabus- or transcript-level disclosure of assessment mode and verification method is operationally and legally feasible at a typical university | current constraint | Accept — expires where registrar/transcript policy does not currently support course-level annotation; syllabus-level disclosure is feasible today regardless | Accept — feasible at the syllabus level now; transcript-level disclosure requires registrar policy change not assumed available everywhere | unverified — flagged (used in C5) |

## 3. Ground Truths

**Reduce-to-primitives pass (five-whys, reduce-to-primitives mode), feeding GT-9.** The compound claim "authorship of a submitted work product can be verified" was decomposed before being trusted: it rests on (a) the format restricting access to unauthorized aid during production, (b) the format allowing direct observation of the production process, and (c) direct observation, where available, disclosing the identity of the cognitive agent producing the work. Constituent (c) is itself reducible: observation directly discloses behavior and presence (measurable), but connecting that behavior to *authorship* requires an inference step, because cognition itself — the process being certified — is private and has no direct external measurement. That inference step does not reduce further; it bottoms out at a definitional/logical primitive about what observation can and cannot disclose. That primitive is recorded below as GT-9. Constituents (a) and (b) remain format-dependent current constraints, not physical laws, and are captured in GT-5 and GT-10? rather than promoted to the same status as GT-9.

- **GT-1** Repeated retrieval practice (testing) produces substantially better long-term retention than repeated restudying: students given repeated tests retained roughly 80% of material after one week, versus roughly 36% for students who only restudied the same material for the same total time — source: Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L. (2007/2008), *Journal of Memory and Language*, "Repeated retrieval during learning is the key to long-term retention"; read-at-source: results section, the paper's headline quantitative retention comparison, read via the Purdue Learning Lab-hosted PDF. Provenance: **read-at-source**.
- **GT-2** Independent (non-vendor) testing of AI-text detectors shows they are unreliable on human-written text, with false-positive rates that are especially severe for non-native-English-speaker writing: a Stanford study (Liang et al., *Patterns*, 2023) found an average 61.3% false-positive rate across seven detectors on 91 TOEFL essays by non-native speakers, versus near-zero false positives on native-speaker eighth-grade essays; Turnitin's own claimed <1% false-positive rate applies only to its internal testing conditions where more than 20% of a document is AI-generated — source: CASRAI, "AI Detector Accuracy: The False-Positive Evidence" (casrai.org/guides/ai-detection-accuracy-higher-education), which quotes and cites the underlying Stanford/Patterns figures; read-at-source: the page's "Key Findings on Non-Native English Speakers" and "Vendor Claims vs. Independent Results" sections, read directly. Provenance: **read-at-source** (for this analysis's citation of the CASRAI page; the CASRAI page in turn cites the Stanford *Patterns* paper, which this analysis did not separately open).
- **GT-3?** As of the current date, LLM writing assistants (e.g., Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) are cheaply or freely accessible to essentially any student with internet access, and can produce competent disciplinary essay-length prose, code, and analysis with no further human skill beyond prompting — unverified: this is stipulated by the problem statement itself and is corroborated only by general background knowledge of consumer LLM deployment since 2022–2023, not by a source opened in this session. Provenance: **unverified**.
- **GT-4?** Contract cheating (paying or otherwise having a third party complete assessments) predates LLMs and was already a nontrivial problem under unsupervised/take-home conditions: self-report prevalence estimates range from roughly 3.5% to 15.7% of surveyed students depending on study and era, and a 2018 estimate put the number of university students worldwide who had paid a third party for some assessment at roughly 31 million — cited to: a systematic review (Frontiers in Education, 2018) and a TEQSA summary, as reported by a web search synthesis in this session; reported-by-delegate: search-result summary, primary sources not opened by this analysis. Provenance: **reported-by-delegate**.
- **GT-5** A timed, proctored written exam is defined by restricting a student's access to external tools, reference material, and collaborators during a bounded assessment window; a take-home assessment, absent additional monitoring technology, does not restrict such access — source: definitional, entailed by the accepted meaning of the two terms as used in this analysis and in the problem statement; no external document to read. Provenance: **definitional** (not applicable to the read-at-source test, which presumes an external document).
- **GT-6?** Educational credentials function as a signal to third parties (employers, licensing boards, graduate programs); the informational value of that signal depends on the assessment's ability to reliably attribute demonstrated performance to the credentialed individual — unverified: standard information-economics/signaling-theory content, not independently sourced in this session. Provenance: **unverified**.
- **GT-7?** Different university courses certify different competencies: some require demonstrated *unaided* performance (e.g., foundational skill-building, licensure-adjacent gatekeeping content), while most knowledge-work-oriented courses certify the ability to produce well-reasoned output using the resources a practitioner would actually have, including reference material, collaborators, and now AI tools — unverified: a reasoned generalization about the structure of academic and professional work, not confirmed against any specific institution's outcomes statements in this session. Provenance: **unverified**. This is the analysis's single most load-bearing ground truth (see Adversarial pass, Sensitivity).
- **GT-8?** Timed, high-stakes testing conditions measurably depress performance for a meaningfully sized subset of test-takers independent of their underlying competence (the test-anxiety effect in educational psychology) — unverified: general disciplinary knowledge, not independently sourced in this session. ## 4. Derivation Chains

**Companion techniques applied in this section:** an inversion pass (Phase 2) tested the claim "take-home assessment validly certifies course competency" against what would guarantee its failure; a theoretical-limit derivation (below, feeding C1) establishes the integrity ceiling either format can reach; two trade-off analyses (below, feeding C2 and C3) weigh timed-exam and take-home variants against a locked, weighted criteria set for two different competency types; and a second-order pass (feeding C4) extends the resulting policy through the actor and time lenses.

**Inversion (Phase 2), applied to "take-home assessment validly certifies course competency."** Inverted: "take-home assessment does not validly certify course competency." Failure-guaranteeing conditions enumerated: (1) the assessed task can be fully completed by AI with no verification step catching non-attributable output; (2) the institution asserts the credential certifies unaided competency while no longer measuring it; (3) no corroborating authorship signal exists at all beyond self-report; (4) the course's certified competency is, in fact, unaided time-pressured performance, and take-home is the wrong format for it; (5) automated detection is relied on as the sole integrity control despite its documented unreliability. Deriving the necessary preconditions for the *original* (un-inverted) claim to hold: **P1** — the course's certified competency does not require unaided, time-pressured performance (load-bearing; this is GT-7?/A6's role); **P2** — at least one non-detector corroborating authorship signal exists (load-bearing; this is GT-10?/A9's role); **P3** — the institution accurately discloses what the credential certifies (load-bearing; this is A16's role). All three preconditions are unverified or current-constraint assumptions already carried in the Assumptions Table (A6, A9, A16), which is why they were not re-added as new rows — the inversion pass confirmed, rather than expanded, the assumption set, and its five failure conditions map directly onto the Adversarial pass's Clusters 1–3 below.

**Theoretical-limit derivation, feeding C1.** Direction: higher is better (more confidence in authorship attribution is the improving direction). Governing constraint: GT-9 — no external observer, proctored or not, can directly observe another person's cognitive process; only behavior and its artifacts are observable. Ideal ceiling: bounded confidence approaching, but never reaching, certainty, achieved by stacking multiple independent behavioral proxies (identity verification, timing, process logs, oral questioning) — never a deductive guarantee. Best demonstrated: in-person, single-proctor timed exams, which in practice achieve high (not perfect) confidence via one dominant proxy — continuous physical presence — and are vulnerable to rare but real defeat conditions (impersonation, concealed devices, leaked questions). Conventional figure (untreated take-home): confidence resting on a single, weak, evadable proxy — automated AI-text detection (GT-2). Gap 1 (conventional → best demonstrated): closeable now, without new technology, by adding any second behavioral proxy (oral defense, process log) — this is exactly what the "redesigned take-home" option in C2 does. Gap 2 (best demonstrated → ideal ceiling): irreducible; no format, including in-person proctoring, closes it, because GT-9 is a constraint on observation itself, not on any particular technology.

### Conclusion C1: No assessment format — timed-proctored or take-home — can guarantee individual authorship; both rely on imperfect proxies for a fact that cannot be directly observed

GT-9 (observation verifies presence and behavior, not cognition) + GT-2 (independent AI-detector false-positive rate ~61% on non-native-speaker writing, near-zero on native writing)
→ in-person proctoring and automated AI-text detection are both inference mechanisms that reason from behavioral proxies to a claim about an unobservable cognitive origin, not direct measurements of that origin
→ because both mechanisms are inferential rather than deductive, the achievable integrity ceiling for any single assessment format is bounded confidence rather than certainty
→ describing timed proctored exams as "guaranteeing" authentic authorship while take-home assessments "cannot" verify it overstates a difference of degree as a difference of kind

**Pre-check:** head GT-9, GT-2 · ?-marked: none · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH — the rival view that proctoring failures are rare enough that "guarantee" is a reasonable approximation for timed exams specifically is addressed by GT-9 directly: the disputed claim is categorical (whether cognition can be directly observed at all), not empirical (how often proctoring fails), so rarity of proctoring failures does not rescue the "guarantee" framing.

**Trade-off analysis, feeding C2 (Type II course: certified competency is producing well-reasoned written work using the resources a practitioner would actually have — e.g., a policy-analysis or case-study seminar).** Options: (a) closed-book timed exam; (b) untreated take-home (open, AI-permitted, no added verification); (c) redesigned take-home (AI use disclosed/permitted, plus a brief oral defense or spot-check and a submitted process log); (d) open-book/open-note timed exam (resources allowed, still time-boxed, no AI). One must-have applied as a knockout, eliminating a fifth candidate: continuous biometric/webcam-and-keystroke monitoring of all take-home work fails "deliverable without infeasible universal surveillance" and is eliminated outright (see Dead End 1, §5) rather than scored. Criteria, weights (1–5, locked before scoring), and anchors: **construct validity** (5) — 1 = format measures a materially different construct than the course claims, 5 = format mirrors the real-world performance conditions of the certified competency; **integrity assurance** (4) — 1 = no attribution signal beyond self-report, 5 = multiple independent corroborating signals; **equity/accessibility** (4) — 1 = large documented disparate impact on a protected/vulnerable group, 5 = no material disparate impact identified; **feasibility/cost** (3) — 1 = requires resources unavailable at current staffing, 5 = deliverable with current staffing; **post-graduation relevance** (3) — 1 = assessment conditions never recur after graduation, 5 = conditions closely mirror professional practice. Scores (cited to GT-7?/A12 for construct validity, GT-2 for integrity, GT-8? and general reasoning about access disparities for equity, A10 for feasibility, GT-7?/GT-11? for post-graduation relevance): (a) 1,5,2,5,1 → 51; (b) 5,1,3,5,5 → 71; (c) 5,4,4,3,5 → 81; (d) 2,5,2,5,2 → 59. Winner: (c), redesigned take-home. Flip test: (c) leads (b) by 10 points, driven by Integrity (+12 weighted) and Equity (+4 weighted) against (b)'s Feasibility lead (−6 weighted); solving for the smallest single-weight change that flips the winner requires raising the Feasibility weight to 8 or dropping Integrity's weight below 1, both outside the 1–5 scale — **no single-criterion weight change within the locked 1–5 scale flips the result.**

### Conclusion C2: For Type II courses, a redesigned take-home assessment outperforms both the closed-book timed exam and an untreated take-home on the weighted framework above

GT-7? (courses certify heterogeneous competencies) + GT-2 (AI-text detectors unreliable, biased against non-native English writers) + C1 (no format achieves certain attribution)
→ for a Type II course the closed-book timed exam scores lowest on construct validity, because it certifies unaided rapid recall, a skill the course does not claim to teach *[Assumes: A12 — a course's own stated learning outcomes are the correct reference point for judging construct validity]*
→ the untreated take-home scores lowest on integrity among the four candidate formats, because it relies on the AI-text detectors GT-2 shows are unreliable as its only corroborating check
→ a redesigned take-home that adds a brief oral defense and a submitted process log raises the integrity score above the untreated take-home's without reintroducing the timed exam's construct mismatch, because the added checks corroborate authorship without restricting resource access
→ across the five weighted criteria the redesigned take-home scores highest at 81 of 100, ahead of the untreated take-home (71), the open-book timed exam (59), and the closed-book timed exam (51), and this ranking is unchanged by any single-criterion weight change within the locked 1–5 scale *[Assumes: A13 — the assigned criterion weights of 5, 4, 4, 3, 3 reflect this institution's actual priorities]*

**Pre-check:** head GT-7?, GT-2, C1 (HIGH) · ?-marked: GT-7? · lowest cited: HIGH · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-7? (that different courses certify different competencies, some requiring unaided performance and some not) is unverified in this analysis; it rests on general professional-practice reasoning rather than a source opened this session. Verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade: coding this institution's own course-level learning-outcomes statements against the Type I/II/III taxonomy used here to confirm the heterogeneity claim empirically. C1 is HIGH and is not a cause of the downgrade.

**Trade-off analysis, feeding C3 (Type I course: certified competency is unaided fluency or rapid judgment under time pressure — e.g., a foundational quantitative-reasoning or licensure-gatekeeping course).** Same four options, same locked criteria and weights, re-anchored to this competency type (construct validity and post-graduation/skill-building relevance now favor unaided, time-boxed performance, since that is what the course certifies). Scores: (a) closed-book timed exam: 5,5,2,5,5 → 83; (b) untreated take-home: 1,1,3,5,1 → 39; (c) redesigned take-home: 2,4,4,3,2 → 57; (d) open-book/open-note timed exam: 4,5,3,5,4 → 79. Winner: (a), closed-book timed exam, but by a narrow four-point margin over (d). Flip test between (a) and (d): the gap is driven almost entirely by construct validity (+5 weighted for (a)) against equity (+4 weighted for (d)); dropping the construct-validity weight from 5 to 1 exactly erases the gap — the smallest weight change available on the 1–5 scale.

### Conclusion C3: For Type I courses, a closed-book timed exam scores highest on the same weighted framework, though only narrowly ahead of an open-book timed exam, and both timed formats clearly outscore either take-home option

GT-1 (retrieval practice: ~80% vs ~36% one-week retention) + GT-7? (courses certify heterogeneous competencies) + GT-8? (timed high-stakes conditions depress performance for a subset of test-takers independent of competence)
→ for a Type I course the closed-book timed exam scores highest on both construct validity and the skill-building criterion, because unaided retrieval practice is the mechanism GT-1 shows builds the durable knowledge base the course exists to establish *[Assumes: A11 — GT-1's testing-effect advantage, established for cued recall, is assumed to transfer to full essay and argument writing]*
→ GT-8? pulls the closed-book exam's equity score down, and an open-book, open-note, still time-boxed and AI-restricted exam recovers most of that equity loss while giving up only a small amount of construct validity
→ the two timed formats score 83 and 79 of 100, a four-point gap that a one-point change to the construct-validity weight is sufficient to erase, so the live choice for a Type I course is between two timed formats, not between timed and take-home *[Assumes: A13 — the assigned criterion weights reflect this institution's actual priorities]*
→ both timed formats outscore the take-home options, at 57 and 39, by a wide and robust margin for this competency type

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-7?, GT-8? · ?-marked: GT-7?, GT-8? · lowest cited: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-7? carries the same unresolved status noted in C2 (see C2's confidence line for the verification path). GT-8? (test-anxiety literature) is unverified in this analysis; the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade is a review of the institution's own accommodated-testing data comparing performance under timed versus extended-time conditions. The *[Assumes: A11]* premise on hop 1 is priced on hop 3: if A11 is false and GT-1's effect does not transfer to essay writing, both timed formats' construct-validity and skill-building scores fall together, which narrows or could reverse the already-narrow 83-vs-79 gap between them, but does not by itself favor either take-home option, since GT-7? — not A11 — is what separates timed from take-home in this framework.

### Conclusion C4: Adopting the differentiated policy (C2 for Type II/III courses, C3 for Type I courses) sets in motion second- and third-order effects that are net favorable only if paired with a resourced verification standard

C2 (redesigned take-home wins for Type II courses) + C3 (timed exam retained for Type I courses) + GT-1 (retrieval practice builds durable retention)
→ faculty asked to run oral-defense or process-log spot-checks face a real, uncompensated workload increase, and departments that do not resource this step will default to the untreated take-home this analysis already ranked lowest on integrity for Type II courses *[Assumes: A10 — verification requires new, currently uncompensated faculty or TA time]*
→ in the near term, students and faculty face inconsistent course-to-course rules about what AI use is permitted, and this inconsistency becomes a source of perceived unfairness independent of which rule any single course adopts
→ if that confusion leads administrators to simplify toward one uniform policy rather than investing further in the distinction, foundational courses lose the timed retrieval practice GT-1 shows builds durable retention *[Assumes: A14 — administrators facing implementation confusion are more likely to simplify toward uniformity than to invest further in maintaining the differentiated policy]*
→ students who lose that foundation arrive at upper-level Type II and Type III coursework less able to critically evaluate AI output against a durable knowledge base, which is the exact failure mode the Type I recommendation in C3 exists to prevent
→ conversely, an institution that keeps the distinction and resources the verification step can credibly signal graduates as both fundamentals-strong and AI-fluent, a competitive position relative to peer institutions that either ban AI outright or adopt it without verification *[Assumes: A15 — employers and prospective students can perceive and value this signal over a generic degree]*

**Pre-check:** head C2 (MEDIUM), C3 (MEDIUM), GT-1 · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by C2 and C3, each MEDIUM (see their own confidence lines for the GT-7?/GT-8?/A11 verification paths). The *[Assumes: A10]* premise on hop 1 is priced by the hop itself, which states the consequence if A10 is not resourced (default to the lower-integrity untreated take-home) rather than assuming it resolves favorably; likewise *[Assumes: A14]* on hop 3 is priced by hops 3–4, which state the consequence chain if the prediction holds rather than assuming it.

### Conclusion C5: A university should adopt a differentiated policy matching assessment format to the specific competency each course certifies, implemented only alongside a resourced, disclosed verification standard

C1 (no format guarantees attribution; both are inferential) + C2 (redesigned take-home wins for Type II courses) + C3 (timed exam retained for Type I courses) + C4 (second/third-order effects favor the distinction only if verification is resourced)
→ because C1 rules out "guaranteed integrity" as the deciding criterion for either format, the decision properly turns on construct validity — which competency a given course actually certifies — and C2 and C3 show that criterion produces opposite winners depending on the course's competency type
→ C4 shows this differentiated policy is stable, and avoids undermining its own Type I branch, only when paired with a minimum institutional verification standard rather than left to unresourced, ad hoc faculty discretion *[Assumes: A16 — syllabus- or transcript-level disclosure of assessment mode and verification method is operationally and legally feasible at a typical university]*
→ the validated policy is conditional: timed, resource-restricted exams for courses whose stated competency is unaided performance under time pressure, and verified, AI-disclosed take-home assessment for courses whose stated competency is producing well-reasoned work with realistic resource access, each adoption requiring a resourced, disclosed verification step

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), C2 (MEDIUM), C3 (MEDIUM), C4 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — capped by C2, C3 and C4, each MEDIUM; C2 and C3's shortfall traces to GT-7? and, for C3 specifically, to GT-8? and the *[Assumes: A11]* premise about GT-1's transfer to essay writing (see C2/C3's own confidence lines for verification paths). C1 is HIGH and is not a cause of the downgrade.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Continuous biometric/webcam-and-keystroke monitoring of all take-home work

**What was tried:** Considered as a fifth trade-off option, on the reasoning that if the concern is unverifiable authorship, the direct fix is continuous identity and behavior monitoring during take-home work, closing most of the gap identified in C1's theoretical-limit derivation.

**Why abandoned:** Eliminated by the trade-off's must-have knockout — it is not deliverable at realistic institutional scale without infeasible cost and privacy exposure (surveillance of students' homes), and it does not close the irreducible gap identified in GT-9 regardless of how much is spent on it, since GT-9's constraint is about observation of cognition, not about the fidelity of behavioral monitoring.

**What it ruled out:** Saves a future reader from re-proposing "just monitor harder" as a solution to the integrity question; GT-9 shows this approach hits a hard ceiling before it reaches certainty, and it fails the feasibility/equity criteria long before that ceiling is relevant.

### Dead End: A blanket return to closed-book, no-device, all-courses timed exams as the integrity fix

**What was tried:** Considered as the mirror-image rival to the naive "switch everything to take-home" plan — if AI availability is the problem, restore full physical proctoring and closed-book conditions everywhere, eliminating AI access at the source.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicts GT-7? for Type II/III courses (construct mismatch — these courses do not claim to certify unaided rapid recall) and A3/GT-11? (fails to prepare students for professional AI-augmented practice, the opposite equity/relevance failure to the one this analysis is trying to avoid). It is not a genuine rival to C5 as a whole; for Type I courses specifically it collapses into C3's own recommendation and adds nothing beyond it.

**What it ruled out:** Saves a future reader from treating "just ban AI everywhere" as a clean universal fix; it is the correct answer only for the subset of courses C3 already identifies, and is a construct-validity failure everywhere else.

### Dead End: Relying primarily on AI-detection software as the integrity backbone for take-home assessments

**What was tried:** Considered as the cheapest, most scalable integrity control for a take-home policy — flag suspected AI-generated submissions automatically and act on the flag.

**Why abandoned:** GT-2 (read at source) shows detector false-positive rates average 61.3% on non-native-English-speaker writing, against near-zero on native-speaker writing, making this control both unreliable and systematically discriminatory if used as a primary, high-stakes signal.

**What it ruled out:** Saves a future reader from treating detector output as sufficient evidence on its own; it is retained in the redesigned take-home option (C2) only as a weak secondary signal, never as the sole basis for an integrity finding (Adversarial pass, Cluster 4 disposition).

---

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Do not choose once, university-wide, between timed written exams and take-home assessments. Retain timed, resource-restricted exams for courses whose stated competency is unaided performance under time pressure, and adopt verified, AI-disclosed take-home assessment — paired with a brief oral defense or process-log check — for courses whose stated competency is producing well-reasoned work with the resources a practitioner would actually have; require a resourced, disclosed verification step as a precondition of every take-home adoption (chain C5).

**Key insight:** The comparison is not "which format is cheat-proof" — no format is (chain C1) — it is "which format matches the specific competency a given course certifies," and that single criterion produces opposite winners for different course types (chains C2, C3), which is why a single global policy is the wrong shape of answer regardless of which one format is chosen.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** The differentiated policy costs administrative consistency — multiple standards across a single transcript — and is only stable if institutions actually resource the verification step; left unresourced, it risks eroding back into a uniform policy that undermines its own foundational-course branch (chain C4). For Type I courses specifically, the margin between the closed-book and open-book timed exams is narrow enough (83 vs. 79) that a reasonable institution could choose either without contradicting this analysis (chain C3).

**Confidence:** MEDIUM — C5 itself is MEDIUM, capped by C2, C3 and C4; see C5's own confidence line, which traces the shortfall to GT-7? and, through C3, to GT-8? and the A11 premise. No `GT-N?` is rested on by the Conclusion directly outside the chains already named. The single change most likely to raise this to HIGH is independently verifying GT-7? — confirming, against this institution's actual course-level learning-outcomes statements, that courses do in fact certify heterogeneous competencies rather than one uniform skill.
